facts.fact: Anubias, Bucephalandra, java fern and mosses are low-light plants, and anubias, Bucephalandra and java fern need no CO2.
For beginners, Aquarium Co-Op suggests slow-growing plants that need low light and little or no fertilizer, such as marimo moss balls, anubias and java fern, none of which need substrate.
Water-column feeders take their nutrients from the water and need regular liquid fertilizer. Plain sand or gravel works for them.
Root feeders such as swords and Cryptocoryne take most of their food from the substrate. In sand or gravel they need root tabs or aqua soil.
Plants sold in tissue-culture cups are free of pests and often settle in quickly.
Cryptocoryne species that grow in hard water are usually easier to keep. Species from peat bogs need soft water and decaying leaf litter.
Cryptocoryne wendtii is described as a very versatile species.
Before planting, remove the rock wool and the plastic pot, except for carpeting plants.
Pick off the small yellow fertilizer balls in the pot so they don't cause a nutrient spike.
Rhizome plants (anubias, java fern, bolbitis): don't bury the rhizome. Attach it to wood or rock with super glue gel or thread, and feed with liquid fertilizer.
Rosette plants (swords, crypts): bury the roots but keep the crown above the substrate. Swords feed heavily through their roots and need root tabs.
Stem plants: remove the band, then plant each stem on its own, 2 to 3 inches deep. Use plant weights if needed.
Bulbs (banana plant, tiger lotus, aponogetons): rinse off any covering and set the bulb on top of the substrate. If nothing grows in 1 to 3 weeks, check whether it is upside down.
Carpeting plants: keep the rock wool, put a root tab in the middle and press the plug into the substrate, or split the pot into 5 to 6 chunks spaced a few inches apart.
Trim sword and Cryptocoryne roots longer than 1.5–2 inches before planting.
Melting means the old leaves die off soon after planting. On plants grown out of water, this is normal: new underwater leaves usually appear within a few weeks.
Yellowing leaves and leaf loss can mean the plant lacks nutrients or light.
Anubias rot is a rare disease that makes the rhizome mushy until it breaks down.
Nurseries often grow plants emersed (leaves in the air), so the leaves melt once the plant is fully under water.
Moving a tank or changing fertilizer, CO2, water changes, lighting or temperature can make plants melt. Crypts are especially prone to this.
Rapid changes in the environment are thought to trigger crypt melt. Some reports also link it to nitrate buildup and advise regular water changes.
A plant that froze or overheated in transit may lose its leaves or die after planting.
Remove melting leaves, don't move the plant, and keep conditions stable. New leaves come in over several weeks.
Crypts may need about 30 days to settle in and regrow leaves after transplanting.
For anubias rot, cut off the affected parts and see whether the rest recovers.
For nutrient shortage, dose a complete fertilizer regularly, use root tabs for root feeders, trim plants that shade others, and use lighting made for plants.
Check that a plant fertilizer contains nitrogen, phosphate and potassium, and keep some phosphate in the water.
To kill hitchhiking snails and their eggs, soak new plants for two days in 1 tablespoon of potassium alum per gallon of water. In a cited test, this did not kill the plants.
In the same test, salt, bleach, potassium permanganate and copper did not kill all snails and snail eggs.
A dip in hydrogen peroxide (a 25% solution of 3% peroxide for one day) killed snails and eggs but seemed to harm the plants.
Alum and carbonated-water dips kill animals. Never use them where fish, shrimp or other livestock are present.
Alum does not kill algae or bacteria. Plants cannot be fully sterilized.
Grow crypts in an aquarium that has been running for at least three months.
Throw away unwanted aquarium plants in a sealed plastic bag in the trash. Never dump them in streams, rivers or ditches, and don't compost them near water.
Hydrilla, once a common aquarium plant, spreads fast and clogs waterways. Water hyacinth is called the world's worst aquatic weed.
Burying the rhizome of anubias, Bucephalandra or java fern.
Covering the crown of a sword or crypt with substrate.
Planting stem plants or grass-like plants as one bunch instead of one at a time.
Planting stem plants with the lead weights still attached.
Throwing out crypts that have melted, when they often regrow underwater leaves.
Pulling a melting sword or crypt out of the substrate. The switch to underwater leaves takes about a month.
Letting floating plants cover the whole surface, which can cut light and oxygen.
Underfeeding plants, which this guide says causes most algae problems in planted tanks.
Using nitrate- or phosphate-removing pads in a planted tank.
Leaving plants in a hot car.
Heat matters in a hot climate: most plants do best under 80°F, and 83–85°F is the upper limit for most species.
Mosses grow best at 68–76°F and decline above 78°F. Moss suits shrimp tanks only in cooler water.
Wikipedia gives Cryptocoryne a temperature range of about 12–33 °C.

Vietnamese shop names: thủy diệp lan = Cryptocoryne; rêu bèo = Riccia fluitans; cây ổ sao cánh = Microsorum pteropus (java fern); cỏ năng = Eleocharis acicularis; rong lá ngò = Cabomba aquatica; rong lá thông = Najas microdon.
Brands of tissue-culture cups often use a colour code for difficulty, with green as the easiest.
Some nurseries ship crypts as bare rootstock, because the leaves are lost after planting anyway.
